# Why this section exists

A model in a notebook is a prototype. A system is what happens when that prototype has to answer real requests, on fresh data, while someone watches whether it is still doing the job.

This wiki already talks about how a model is trained, how it is evaluated, how a language model is served at inference time, and how RAG retrieves before it generates. System design is the layer that ties those pieces together: what problem is worth a model, how data reaches it, how training and serving are kept apart, and what fails when traffic, latency or the world itself changes.

The section has two parts, in this order. **ML system design comes first**, because that is the work this wiki is built around. **General system design comes second**, because an ML service still sits on the same ideas as any other service: load, caches, queues, databases and consistency.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Problem framing"] --> B["Data pipelines"]
  B --> C["Train vs serve"]
  C --> D["Feature store"]
  D --> E["Evaluate"]
  E --> F["Monitor"]
  F --> G["LLM / RAG serving"]
  G --> H["Scale, cache, queues"]
```

# Part 1 — ML system design

These are the pages I intend to write here. None of them exist yet, except as links to work already done elsewhere.

## Problem framing

Not every useful prediction needs a learned model. Sometimes a rule, a query or a simpler statistical baseline is enough, cheaper, and easier to explain. A first page should ask: what is the decision, what is the cost of being wrong, and is machine learning the right tool? This sits next to [What is machine learning](/machine/machine-index.qmd), which already covers the decision / error / optimisation loop.

## Data pipelines

Training data is collected, cleaned, labelled and versioned long before a training job starts. Serving data has to look like that training data, or the model quietly degrades. The [Data](/bigdata/bigdata-index.qmd) section currently holds a Big Data overview; pipelines, freshness and training–serving skew belong here once they are written.

## Training versus serving

Two different jobs, often mistaken for one. Training is slow, batchy and allowed to retry. Serving is latency-bound and has to stay up. [MLOps](/mlops/mlops-index.qmd) is where I will write how code is structured, how a run is repeated, and how train and serve differ as a practice. This section will use that distinction, not repeat it, and then follow the request as it travels through features, the model and a response.

## Feature stores

A feature used at training time has to be available, with the same definition, at serving time. A feature store is the shared catalogue and the serving path for those values — point-in-time correctness for training, low-latency lookups for inference. That page will live here.

## Online and offline evaluation

[Model evaluation](/evaluation/evaluation-index.qmd) is the home for splits, metrics, overfitting and cross-validation. What this section adds is the system question: the offline test that says a new model is better, and the online test (a canary, an A/B experiment, a shadow run) that asks whether it is better for live users.

## Monitoring

Once a model is in production it can fail without crashing. Data drift, concept drift, a silent drop in precision, a feature that stopped arriving — these are system failures. Monitoring here means watching inputs, outputs and business metrics, not only CPU.

## LLM and RAG serving

Language models and retrieval pipelines have their own serving shape: prefill and decode, context windows, index freshness, fallback when retrieval is empty. The model internals are already written — [language-model inference](/generative/language-model-inference.qmd), [why RAG](/rag/why-rag.qmd), [indexing](/rag/rag-indexing.qmd), [retrieval](/rag/rag-retrieval.qmd), [agentic RAG](/rag/agentic-rag.qmd) and [failure modes](/rag/rag-failure-modes.qmd). A later page here will talk about deploying that stack: batching, caching generations, keeping an index in sync, and what to measure when the “model” is a pipeline.

# Part 2 — General system design

An ML service is still a service. These topics are not ML-specific, but they decide whether the service holds under load. Pages I intend to write:

| Topic | What the page should make clear |
|---|---|
| Scalability | Vertical versus horizontal growth, and where a bottleneck actually sits. |
| Load balancing | How requests are spread, and what happens when one replica is slow or dead. |
| Caching | What is safe to remember, for how long, and how a stale cache becomes a wrong answer. |
| Queues | Turning a spike of work into a backlog that can be drained, with retries and dead letters. |
| Databases | When a row store, a document store, a warehouse or a vector index is the right tool. |
| Consistency | What a reader is allowed to see after a write — strong, eventual, and the trade-off with availability. |
